rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.3 - field sampling of salt crusts (EC, thickness, moisture) along the shelterbelt and at the research station in 2012-2013. Q2: Section 3.1/Fig 3 - salt accumulated at the surface during the 10-day drip cycle, crust re-formed on day 4; Section 3.3/Fig 5 - EC lowest near emitter, highest at 40 cm, i.e. salt redistributed outward to the wetting front; Section 3.2/Fig 4 - crust EC and thickness rose with irrigation water salinity. Q4: Section 3.1/Fig 3A - soil water content at 0-30 cm measured daily alongside EC, showing moisture depletion and salt accumulation occurring simultaneously (evaporation-driven mechanism). Q6: Sections 2.1, 2.2.2, 3.2 - crust EC/thickness reported for nine sites (each 4 km long) along the 436 km shelterbelt irrigated with groundwater of different salinities. Q7: Section 3.1 and 4.1/5 - crusts formed once surface EC reached ~1.03 dS/m and moisture fell to ~0.6%; authors state the arid, low-humidity, high-evaporative-demand climate and saline irrigation water are what cause crust formation. Q8: Section 2.1 - only the research station has meteorological data, so authors assume the station and the whole shelterbelt share one climate; Section 4.1 - EC-thickness regressions for 7- and 10-year belts are not robust; Section 4.3 - ion composition and soil properties not examined. Q9: Figs 4, 6, 7 - error bars show one standard deviation of five replicates.
rows.notes: The first half of the passage (evaporation inhibition efficiencies 33.0% vs 13.8%) belongs to ref [54], not this study; this study only cites evaporation reduction by crusts from other work. The study's own result is the salt accumulation/redistribution around emitters. Q7 is borderline: climate and salinity are stated as causes rather than formally as requirements. Q6 judged yes because crust accumulation is reported across the multi-site shelterbelt scheme; the emitter-scale redistribution itself is plot-scale.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2.3, 2.3 - crust samples taken at 10 cm intervals in eight radial directions around five emitters on flat sand and five on 15-25 degree south-facing dune slopes, June 2013. Q2: Section 3.3/Fig 5B - on the dune slope high EC appeared 20-30 cm upslope of the emitter but 40-50 cm downslope; EC upslope higher than downslope; on flat land EC highest to the south and lowest to the north, peak at 40 cm.
rows.notes: Single sampling method (crust EC from field samples). Soil moisture was not measured around emitters on the slope; the gravity-driven wetting-front explanation in Section 4.2 is asserted, not measured. Result comes from ten emitters near the research station only; slope angle inconsistency (15-25 degrees in methods, 32 degrees in results) is not discussed as a limitation. Fig 5 shows spatial averages as contour maps without dispersion measures. Slope/topography is a factor the pattern varied with, not a stated requirement.

notes: Full text available, with some OCR duplication of lines but all sections readable. Study is a field observational study of salt crust EC and thickness under high-salinity drip irrigation in the Taklimakan Desert Highway Shelterbelt.
